investment_summary:
Amazon grew net sales 12% to $716.9 billion in 2025, with AWS up 20% and operating margin up to 11.2% [1]. Normalized income rose 7% to $65.4 billion, because reported EPS was lifted by a $15.3 billion net gain in other income [1]. Cash generation weakened: free cash flow fell 71% to $11.2 billion as cash capital expenditures reached $128.3 billion [1].

The valuation depends on that spending earning returns. The reverse DCF implies 19.3% annual revenue growth over ten years, above consensus growth of 15.7% for FY2026 and 15.8% for FY2027, and well above the 11.7% three-year historical CAGR [2][3]. On consensus numbers, the implied IRR is 8.3%, below the 12.4% WACC used in the model [3]. The current price therefore requires growth above both consensus and history.

Consensus rates the stock Buy with a $326.34 target price [3]. The main risks are fixed-cost capacity, intense competition, and open FTC and tax matters [1]. Consensus and balance-sheet data are dated after the 10-K.
key_takeaways: AWS growth should keep carrying earnings, because AWS sales rose 20% to $128.7 billion with a 35.4% operating margin [1].
Free cash flow must recover before the valuation holds: it fell 71% to $11.2 billion as capex reached $128.3 billion [1].
The price already needs faster growth than history: the reverse DCF implies 19.3% revenue growth versus 15.7% consensus [2][3].
Fixed costs and open regulatory matters are the main downside: much of the cost base is fixed and FTC and tax cases remain unresolved [1].
business_overview:
Amazon.com, Inc. is a retailer and technology company with three reportable segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS) [1]. It sells hundreds of millions of products online and through physical stores, runs a third-party seller marketplace and fulfillment network, and provides cloud computing, advertising, and subscription services [1]. Its Prime membership bundles fast, free shipping with video, live sports, and other benefits, and the company also designs devices such as Kindle, Fire, Echo, Ring, and eero [1]. Management states that low prices and fast delivery are central to the strategy, and the company employed about 1,576,000 people at year-end 2025 [1].

Net sales rose 12% to $716.9 billion in 2025 from $638.0 billion [1]. North America, the largest segment at 59% of sales, grew 10% to $426.3 billion on unit sales, advertising, and subscriptions, and its operating income rose 19% to $29.6 billion, lifting its margin to about 7.0% from 6.4% [1]. International grew 13% to $161.9 billion, but foreign exchange contributed $903 million of its $4.75 billion operating income, so the underlying gain was much smaller [1]. AWS grew 20% to $128.7 billion, driven by customer usage and partly offset by pricing changes in long-term contracts [1].

Costs are rising alongside revenue. Shipping costs rose to $102.7 billion from $95.8 billion, and cash capital expenditures of $128.3 billion, up from $77.7 billion, mainly support AWS infrastructure [1]. Management is also widening the portfolio beyond retail. It invested $2.7 billion in Anthropic convertible notes, and a price adjustment on that stake produced most of a $15.2 billion gain in other income [1]. It is developing a satellite broadband network and autonomous ride-hailing vehicles, and plans quick commerce and sharper international prices in 2026 [1]. The consensus rating is Buy, with a target price of $326.34 [3].
market_position:
Amazon's revenue is concentrated in its home market and in cloud demand, as the segment split shows. North America generated 59% of 2025 net sales ($426.3 billion), International 23% ($161.9 billion), and AWS 18% ($128.7 billion) [1]. The filing does not disclose market share for any segment, so the company's position has to be judged from scale, growth, and margins rather than from a share figure [1]. The filing also gives no customer concentration data, so the 10-K cannot show whether its major customers are blue-chip companies [1]. On the evidence available, Amazon is a large, diversified platform with a strong scale position, though its share is not verified by disclosed market data.

The competitive set differs by segment. The filing names competitors ranging from retailers and cloud providers to search engines and healthcare providers, and notes that some rivals have greater resources, longer histories, and stronger brand recognition [1]. It also says AI and search technologies ease comparison shopping and lower the barrier to entry for smaller rivals [1]. In retail, that pressure shows up in the company's stated need to keep prices low. In cloud, the filing ties AWS growth to customer usage, while pricing changes in long-term contracts weigh on revenue per unit [1].

Market sentiment is supportive but cautious. The consensus rating is Buy with a $326.34 target price, against a 52-week range of $161.38 to $258.60 [2][3]. Consensus FY2026 revenue of $829.2 billion implies growth of 15.7%, slightly above the 12.4% reported for 2025 [1][3]. Current-year EPS consensus fell 0.2% over 90 days, while next-year EPS consensus rose 1.5%, so analysts are not yet raising near-term earnings expectations [3]. These consensus figures are dated after the 10-K.
operating_results:
Net sales rose 12% to $716.9 billion in 2025, and gross margin improved to 50.3% from 48.9% as cost of sales grew 9%, slower than sales [1]. Technology and infrastructure spending rose 23% and is the main cost pressure [1]. Operating income rose to $80.0 billion from $68.6 billion, and operating margin edged up to 11.2% from 10.8%, even after $5.2 billion of FTC settlement and severance charges [1][2]. Diluted EPS rose to $7.17 from $5.53, but that figure includes a $15.3 billion net gain in other income, mostly from the Anthropic stake. Normalized income rose 7% to $65.4 billion and is the better measure of operating earnings growth [1].

Segment results show where the improvement came from. North America's operating income rose 19% to $29.6 billion [1]. International's operating income rose 25% to $4.75 billion, but excluding a $903 million foreign-exchange benefit, the gain was about 1.5% [1]. AWS's operating income rose 14% to $45.6 billion, but its margin slipped to 35.4% from 37.0% as infrastructure spending absorbed much of its sales growth [1]. First-quarter 2026 operating income guidance of $16.5 billion to $21.5 billion compares with $18.4 billion a year earlier, which signals limited near-term earnings momentum [1]. Consensus expects FY2026 GAAP EPS of $12.80 and FY2027 EPS of $10.67, a fall of about 17% that the consensus data does not explain [3].

Cash generation is the weak point. Operating cash flow rose to $139.5 billion from $115.9 billion, but cash capital expenditures reached $128.3 billion, up from $77.7 billion, so free cash flow fell 71% to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion [1]. Cash taxes fell to $8.3 billion from $12.3 billion under the 2025 Tax Act, which flattered operating cash flow [1]. Liquidity held steady, with a current ratio of 1.05 and cash and marketable securities of $123.0 billion, while long-term debt rose to $65.6 billion from $52.6 billion [1][2]. Equity grew 44% to $411.1 billion, lowering total debt to equity to 0.37 from 0.46 [1].
risk_assessment:
The filing identifies three main risks, all of which the 10-K describes as interlocking [1]. The first is competition. The filing states that some rivals have greater resources, longer histories, and stronger brand recognition, and that competition may force Amazon to increase spending or lower prices, either of which "could materially reduce our sales and profits" [1]. The risk is spread across retail, cloud, advertising, and logistics rather than concentrated in one line of business [1]. The filing gives no market-share or pricing data to size it, so the exposure can only be tracked through reported margins.

The second risk is the cost base. The filing says "a significant portion of our expenses and investments is fixed," and that forecasting errors can leave excess or insufficient fulfillment and data-center capacity, which leads to impairment charges [1]. This matters more now because capex has risen sharply. Cash capex reached $128.3 billion, free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion, and the 2025 cash tax benefit of $8.3 billion may not repeat [1][2]. The filing gives no impairment figures, so the scale of this risk cannot be measured from the 10-K alone.

The third risk is legal, regulatory, and tax exposure. The 10-K describes open competition and consumer-protection investigations, litigation brought by state attorneys general and the Federal Trade Commission, and an Indian tax assertion over cloud-service fees [1]. Amazon recorded a $2.5 billion FTC settlement charge in 2025 [1]. On the quality side, the Altman Z-Score of 5.79 and Beneish M-Score of -2.59 do not signal distress or manipulation, though the Piotroski score of 6 of 9 shows some weakening [2]. Year-end net cash was negative $30.0 billion, so the balance sheet relies on continued access to debt markets [2]. Consensus is Buy with a $326.34 target [3]. These consensus and balance-sheet figures are dated after the 10-K.
competitors_analysis:
Amazon was compared with Microsoft, Alphabet, and Walmart. The three peers were chosen on business model first, then size. Microsoft is the closest match to AWS in cloud infrastructure, Alphabet competes with Amazon in advertising and cloud, and Walmart is the largest pure-play retail rival. Their revenue is 0.4x, 0.6x, and 0.9x of Amazon's, so all three are comparable in scale. Coupang, eBay, and Etsy were excluded because they are far smaller and have less comparable models [4].

On growth and profitability, Amazon's 2025 revenue growth of 12.4% trailed Microsoft's 14.9% and Alphabet's 15.1%, and was ahead of Walmart's 5.1% [1][4]. Amazon's gross margin of 50.3% was well below Microsoft's 68.8% and Alphabet's 59.7%, though far above Walmart's margin of roughly 24 to 25% [4]. The EBITDA margin gap was wider still. Amazon's 23.1% compares with 55.2% at Microsoft, 44.9% at Alphabet, and 6.2% at Walmart [4]. Return on invested capital of 16.8% sits below Microsoft's 26.8% and Alphabet's 28.7%, and slightly below Walmart's 17.1% [4].

Cash conversion is the weakest comparison. The competitor tool reports Amazon's FCF conversion at 0.10 for 2025, the lowest of the four companies, against 0.70 at Microsoft, 0.55 at Alphabet, and 0.65 at Walmart [4]. This figure does not reconcile with a simple FCF-to-EBITDA calculation, which gives about 5%, so the exact level should be verified before it is relied on. Even so, both measures point the same way: Amazon converts less of its earnings into cash than its peers. The stock's EV/EBITDA of 15.4x is the lowest of the four, against 24.0x for Microsoft, 21.1x for Alphabet, and 20.0x for Walmart [4]. The market therefore prices Amazon at a discount, which is consistent with weaker cash conversion and the capex burden. Whether that discount is justified depends on whether AWS returns on the spending converge toward Microsoft's and Alphabet's levels.

investment_theses.thesis: AWS keeps compounding fast enough to fund the capex build-out.
investment_theses.evidence: AWS net sales rose 20% to $128.7 billion and operating income rose 14% to $45.6 billion, but margin slipped to 35.4% from 37.0% [1].
investment_theses.signpost: AWS sales growth of at least 18% and operating margin of at least 35% in each 2026 quarterly report.
investment_theses.invalidation: AWS growth below 15% or operating margin below 33% in any 2026 quarter.

investment_theses.thesis: Capex peaks and free cash flow recovers in 2026.
investment_theses.evidence: Cash capex reached $128.3 billion and free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion, while the 2025 tax change cut cash taxes to $8.3 billion from $12.3 billion [1].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 free cash flow above $25 billion in the February 2027 10-K, with capex growth slowing.
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 free cash flow at or below the 2025 level of $11.2 billion, or new borrowing used to fund operations.

investment_theses.thesis: The valuation requires above-trend growth, so returns are exposed to any slowdown.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 19.3% revenue growth for ten years versus 15.7% consensus and an 11.7% historical CAGR; the implied IRR of 8.3% is below the 12.4% WACC [2][3].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 reported revenue at or above the $829 billion consensus in the February 2027 10-K.
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 revenue growth below 15%, which would leave the implied IRR further below the WACC.

investment_theses.thesis: Regulatory and legal costs stay contained relative to the earnings base.
investment_theses.evidence: The 2025 results included $5.2 billion of FTC settlement and severance charges, and cash and marketable securities were $123.0 billion at year-end [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: No new settlement or tax reserve above $2.5 billion disclosed in 2026 filings.
investment_theses.invalidation: A new material FTC settlement or an adverse ruling in the Indian cloud-services tax case.
